hero.caption: A weir chamber of the Croton Aqueduct in Sleepy Hollow, New York. These chambers – another is located in Ossining, New York – were used to empty the aqueduct for maintanece by diverting the water to a nearby waterway, in this case the Pocantico River.  The line could be emptied in as little as two hours, according to a descriptive display at the Ossining chamber. The aqueduct is no longer in use for water delivery, and the right-of-way is now a New York State Historic Park used for walking, jogging and bicycling.

images.caption: The hamlet of Archville along the original Croton Aqueduct route was founded as a community of laborers building the Croton Aqueduct. It was named after an arched bridge that carried the aqueduct over the highway, present-day U.S. Route 9. Built in 1839 and demolished in 1924 as a traffic hazard, the Archville Bridge is commemorated on two plaques on the western end of the pedestrian, trail-walking bridge that later replaced it.
